Incorrect: the key is valid, because the supplier confirms that the card path requires the same key the tool calls use. Regenerating it would not change the anonymous card request. Rotate keys when one is compromised or expires.
Incorrect: the connection uses key-based authentication, so role assignments on the agent identity are not evaluated by the supplier service. Assign roles when the connection uses agent identity.

Incorrect: the credential name must match the header that the endpoint expects, such as x-api-key or Authorization, but the failure is on the card request, which sends no credential at all. Fix the name when tool calls return 401.

stem:
You need to configure how AccountsAgent authenticates to ProfileService.

Which authentication method should you use?
choices: Project managed identity (project-managed-identity) that is granted access to ProfileService
OAuth identity passthrough that uses a custom Microsoft Entra app registration
Agent identity (agentic-identity) of AccountsAgent that is granted access to ProfileService
Key-based authentication that stores an API key for ProfileService in a project connection
explanation: Foundry offers several A2A authentication methods: agent identity, project managed identity, key-based, and OAuth identity passthrough. Agent identity gives per-agent, secretless, app-only access, which makes it the choice when one agent needs access that its sibling agents must not have.
rationale: Incorrect: the project managed identity is shared by every agent in Project1, so granting it access to ProfileService gives the same access to all agents, which the requirements forbid. Use it when all agents in a project need the same access.

Incorrect: identity passthrough calls ProfileService with each signed-in user's access, but the requirement is to use the access of AccountsAgent itself. Use passthrough when per-user permissions must apply at the target endpoint.

Correct: in the new agent object model each agent has its own Microsoft Entra agent identity, so only AccountsAgent is granted access to ProfileService. The call is app-only with the agent's own access, and there are no secrets to store or rotate.

Incorrect: an API key in a project connection is a shared secret that must be stored and rotated, which the technical requirements prohibit. Use key-based authentication only for endpoints that accept nothing else, such as a third-party key-only A2A endpoint.

stem:
Best For You Organics Company wants Agent1, a Foundry prompt agent in Project1, to call Agent2, a Foundry agent in Project2, by using A2A protocol version 1.0. Incoming A2A is already enabled on Agent2, and the identity of Agent1 already has the Foundry Agent Consumer role on Project2. The call must use the identity of Agent1, not the identity of the signed-in user.

Which five actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `azd ai connection create agent2-conn --kind remote-a2a --target <Agent2 A2A base path> --auth-type user-entra-token --audience https://ai.azure.com`
`a2a_connection = project.connections.get("agent2-conn")`
`azd ai project set <Project1 endpoint>`
`azd ai project set <Project2 endpoint>`

`project.agents.create_version(agent_name="Agent1", definition=PromptAgentDefinition(model="gpt-5-mini", tools=[A2ATool(a2a_version=A2AProtocolVersion.V1_0, project_connection_id=a2a_connection.id)]))`
`azd ai connection create agent2-conn --kind remote-a2a --target <Agent2 A2A base path> --auth-type agentic-identity --audience https://ai.azure.com`
`openai.responses.create(tool_choice="required", input="What can Agent2 do?", extra_body={"agent_reference": {"name": "Agent1", "type": "agent_reference"}})`
explanation: To call one Foundry agent from another over A2A, the target needs incoming A2A and the caller needs the Foundry Agent Consumer role on the target project. On the calling project you create a remote-a2a connection to the target's A2A base path with audience https://ai.azure.com, then attach an A2A tool that references the connection. The auth type decides whose identity is used: agentic-identity for app-only, user-entra-token for delegated calls.
rationale: Incorrect: user-entra-token passes the signed-in user's Microsoft Entra context to Agent2, which breaks the requirement to call as Agent1. Use it for existing delegated integrations that need the user context.
Step 3: the SDK reads the connection by name to get its full id. The A2A tool definition in the next step needs this connection id, so the connection must already exist in Project1.
Step 1: azd ai commands act on the active project. The connection belongs to the calling side, so Project1 must be the active project before you create it.
Incorrect: setting Project2 as the active project would create the connection in the target project, where Agent1 cannot use it. Set Project2 only when you configure resources for Agent2 itself.
Step 4: create_version() adds an A2ATool for protocol version 1.0 that references the connection id, so Agent1 can delegate tasks to Agent2 through the connection and its identity.
Step 2: a remote-a2a connection that targets the A2A base path of Agent2 with agentic-identity and the https://ai.azure.com audience makes the call app-only with the identity of Agent1.
Step 5: a request with tool_choice set to required forces Agent1 to call the A2A tool, which tests the delegation end to end after everything else exists.

stem:
Litware, Inc. connects a Foundry agent to a third-party A2A endpoint that accepts only a static API key. All users of the agent share the same level of access. The security team requires that exposure of the shared secret is minimized.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Store the API key in a project connection and restrict who can access the project
Request a least-privilege key from the endpoint publisher and rotate it before it expires
Set send_credentials_for_agent_card to true so that every request carries the key
Configure OAuth identity passthrough so that each user signs in to the endpoint
Configure the A2A connection to authenticate by using the project managed identity
explanation: When an A2A endpoint accepts only a static API key and all users share the same access, the key is unavoidable. Reduce its exposure by storing it in a project connection with limited access, and by requesting a least-privilege key that you rotate regularly.
rationale: Correct: a project connection stores the key securely instead of in code, and restricting who can access the project limits who can read or use the secret.
Correct: a least-privilege key limits the damage if it leaks, and rotating it before it expires shortens the window in which a leaked key can be used.
Incorrect: send_credentials_for_agent_card sends the key on the agent card request as well, which adds exposure. Set it only when the endpoint requires authentication to read its card.

Incorrect: OAuth identity passthrough needs an endpoint that supports OAuth, but this endpoint accepts only a static key. Use passthrough when each user must access the endpoint with the user's own identity.
Incorrect: project managed identity authentication requires an endpoint that accepts Microsoft Entra tokens, so it cannot authenticate to a key-only endpoint. Use it for Entra-protected endpoints.

stem:
Graphic Design Institute has a Foundry prompt agent named ReviewAgent that has incoming A2A enabled. An existing partner agent that is built with the open-source A2A SDK calls ReviewAgent by using A2A v1.0 over JSONRPC. Integration tests show the following behavior:

- Requests that contain only text parts succeed.
- Requests that attach design files as file parts fail.
- The partner client is configured to receive server-sent events and never receives incremental updates.

You need to make the integration work without changing how ReviewAgent is hosted.

What should you do?
choices: Send the design content as text and configure the partner client for non-streaming requests.
Switch the partner client to A2A v0.3 with the HTTP+JSON transport to support file parts.
Switch the partner client to the gRPC transport to support streaming and binary parts.
Assign the partner identity the Foundry User role instead of the Foundry Agent Consumer role.
explanation: Incoming A2A on a Foundry agent supports A2A v1.0 over JSON-RPC with text parts only, and streaming responses are not supported. Existing partner clients must send text and use non-streaming requests; protocol or transport changes do not add these capabilities.
rationale: Correct: incoming A2A supports text modality only and no streaming, so the partner must send the design content as text and call ReviewAgent without server-sent events.
Incorrect: the preview v0.3 protocol is also limited to text on Foundry agent targets, so switching versions does not enable file parts. Use v0.3 only for existing preview integrations.
Incorrect: incoming A2A on a Foundry agent uses JSON-RPC, so a gRPC transport is not available and would not add streaming or binary parts. Use gRPC only with A2A servers that offer it.
Incorrect: Foundry Agent Consumer is enough to call the agent, because text requests already succeed. Changing roles affects authorization, not supported content types or streaming.

stem:
Humongous Insurance builds an orchestrator agent that must select, invoke, filter, and weigh the results of internal claims capabilities, and then synthesize the final answer itself. The capabilities are owned by the same engineering team as the orchestrator. The architects prefer control over the reasoning to flexibility, and they require authenticated access to the underlying tools and data.

Which integration approach should you use?
choices: Expose the claims capabilities through MCP servers that the orchestrator calls as tools
Expose each claims capability as an A2A agent that uses its own orchestration
Register each claims capability in Foundry Control Plane as a custom A2A agent
Connect the claims capabilities as handoff targets that take ownership of the conversation
explanation: Choose MCP when an orchestrator must stay in control of the reasoning and call capabilities as tools that it selects, filters, and combines itself. Choose A2A when capabilities are autonomous agents with their own orchestration, often owned by other teams.
rationale: Correct: MCP servers expose the claims capabilities as tools, so the orchestrator selects, invokes, filters, and weighs the results and keeps control of the reasoning, and MCP supports authenticated access.
Incorrect: A2A agents run their own orchestration and return finished answers, so the orchestrator loses control over how each capability reasons. Use A2A for autonomous agents owned by other teams.

Incorrect: registering custom A2A agents in Foundry Control Plane adds governance and a proxy, but the capabilities still reason on their own. Use it to manage A2A agents that run outside Agent Service.
Incorrect: handoff targets take ownership of the conversation, so the orchestrator could not synthesize the final answer. Use handoff when a specialist should own the rest of the conversation.

stem:
Adventure Works Cycles automates warranty processing. The process has well-defined steps, and several agents and deterministic functions must coordinate in an explicit order that the developers control.

Which Microsoft Agent Framework component should you use?
choices: A workflow
A single agent with function tools
Agent middleware
A context provider
explanation: Agent Framework distinguishes agents, which plan and call tools autonomously, from workflows, which coordinate agents and functions in an explicit, developer-defined order. Use a workflow when the process has well-defined steps; use an agent when the task is open-ended.
rationale: Correct: a workflow connects agents and deterministic functions as executors with explicit edges, so the developers control the order of the well-defined warranty steps.
Incorrect: a single agent with function tools lets the model decide which tools to call and in which order, so the developers do not control the order. Use it for open-ended or conversational tasks.
Incorrect: agent middleware intercepts runs to add logging, checks, or result changes. It does not coordinate several agents and functions in order. Use it for cross-cutting concerns.
Incorrect: a context provider adds memories or extra context to an agent before each run. It does not define execution order. Use it to enrich prompts with relevant context.

stem:
Trey Research has production multi-agent solutions built with Semantic Kernel and AutoGen. The company wants to standardize on the framework that the same Microsoft teams created as the direct successor to both, including graph-based workflows.

Which framework should you choose?
choices: Microsoft Agent Framework
LangGraph
Microsoft 365 Agents SDK
LangChain
explanation: Microsoft Agent Framework is the direct successor of Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, built by the same Microsoft teams. It combines agent abstractions with graph-based workflows and provides migration guides from both frameworks.
rationale: Correct: Agent Framework was created by the Semantic Kernel and AutoGen teams as their direct successor, and it includes graph-based workflows, so it is the standard to migrate both solutions to.
Incorrect: LangGraph is an open-source graph framework from the LangChain ecosystem, not the successor of Semantic Kernel or AutoGen. Use it when the team standardizes on LangChain tooling.
Incorrect: the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK builds agents for channels such as Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot. It is not the successor of Semantic Kernel and AutoGen orchestration.

Incorrect: LangChain is an open-source framework for LLM applications and chains, not a Microsoft successor to Semantic Kernel or AutoGen. Use it with langchain-azure-ai when the team already builds on LangChain.

stem:
Fourth Coffee configures its agents centrally in the Foundry portal. A developer builds a LangGraph application in Python and must use an existing Foundry agent named menu-agent as a node in a graph, without redefining the agent in code. A StateGraph object named workflow is already defined in the application.

Which five actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `workflow.add_node("menu_node", menu_node)`, and then `workflow.add_edge(START, "menu_node")`
`factory.delete_agent(menu_node)`
`factory = AgentServiceFactory(project_endpoint=os.environ["AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT"], credential=DefaultAzureCredential())`
`app = workflow.compile()`
`pip install langchain-azure-ai[tools,opentelemetry] azure-identity`
`menu_node = factory.create_prompt_agent(name="menu-agent", model=os.environ["MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME"], instructions=menu_instructions)`
`menu_node = factory.get_agent_node(name="menu-agent", version="latest")`
explanation: The langchain-azure-ai package bridges LangGraph and Foundry Agent Service through AgentServiceFactory. Referencing portal-managed agents with get_agent_node keeps configuration centralized in Foundry, while create_prompt_agent defines agents in code. Either way, the node is added to a StateGraph and the graph is compiled before it can run.
rationale: Step 4: the node must be added to the StateGraph and connected with edges before compile(), because compile() validates and freezes the graph structure.
Incorrect: delete_agent() removes the agent from the Foundry project, after which the graph object can no longer be used. Use it only to clean up agents you created during a session.
Step 2: AgentServiceFactory connects to the Foundry project. Every agent node that you reference or create later is resolved through this factory object and its credential.
Step 5: compile() turns the StateGraph into a runnable app that you can invoke. It is the last step because it validates the graph and needs all nodes and edges in place.

Step 1: the langchain-azure-ai package provides AgentServiceFactory and the Foundry integration for LangGraph, and azure-identity provides DefaultAzureCredential. Nothing can be imported before they are installed.

Incorrect: create_prompt_agent() defines a new agent version in code, which is exactly what the requirement forbids. Use it when the agent configuration should live in your application code, such as for prototyping.
Step 3: get_agent_node() returns the existing portal-managed agent as a LangGraph-compatible node, so the configuration stays in Foundry; version latest targets the newest version.

stem:
Alpine Ski House builds a LangGraph StateGraph with a local router_node and an expert_node that runs a Foundry agent. The function route_decision must return expert_node when the router delegates and must finish the graph otherwise. The graph must call expert_node only when the router decides to delegate.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

```python
def route_decision(state: RouterState) -> Literal["expert_node", END]:
    if state.get("jump_to") == "delegate":
        return "expert_node"
    return [[1]]

workflow = StateGraph(RouterState)
workflow.add_node("router_node", router_node)
workflow.add_node("expert_node", expert_node)
workflow.add_edge(START, "router_node")
workflow.[[2]]("router_node", route_decision)
workflow.add_edge("expert_node", END)
app = workflow.compile()
```

targets.label: Box 1
why: Correct: END is the special LangGraph node that finishes the graph, so a request the router handles itself ends without calling the Foundry agent or using its tokens.
Incorrect: START is the entry point of the graph and cannot be a routing target. You use it only as the source of the first edge, as in add_edge(START, "router_node").
Incorrect: returning router_node routes back to the router itself, which creates a loop on the same request. Route back to a node only when it must run again, for example in a retry loop.

targets.label: Box 2
why: Incorrect: add_edge creates a fixed edge between two nodes that is always taken, so it cannot choose between expert_node and END. Use it for unconditional steps, such as expert_node to END.
Incorrect: add_node registers a node, not a transition. Registering route_decision as a node would leave router_node without an outgoing edge that depends on the decision.
Correct: add_conditional_edges runs route_decision after router_node and follows the node name it returns, so expert_node runs only when the router delegates.

explanation: In LangGraph, fixed transitions use add_edge and dynamic routing uses add_conditional_edges with a function that returns the next node name or END. A Foundry agent node from get_agent_node behaves like any other node, so you can combine local routing logic with Foundry agents in one graph.

stem:
Relecloud creates a LangGraph agent by using AgentServiceFactory.create_prompt_agent with an MCPTool whose require_approval is set to always and a MemorySaver checkpointer. The first invoke call uses config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "session-7"}} and returns an interrupt for an MCP approval request. The reviewer approves the call.

What should you do to resume the run?
choices: Invoke the agent with Command(resume={"approve": True}) and the same config
Invoke the agent with a new HumanMessage that contains the text approve and no config
Invoke the agent with Command(resume={"approve": True}) and a new thread_id
Send a new request that sets previous_response_id to the interrupt ID
explanation: LangGraph human-in-the-loop uses interrupts and a checkpointer. The run pauses with an interrupt, and you resume it by invoking the graph with Command(resume=...) and the same thread_id, so the checkpointer restores the paused state.
rationale: Correct: Command(resume={"approve": True}) supplies the approval to the pending interrupt, and the same config with thread_id session-7 lets MemorySaver restore the paused run and execute the MCP call.
Incorrect: a new HumanMessage without config starts a new run with no thread, so the paused interrupt is never resumed. Send a new message when the user starts a new turn in an existing thread.
Incorrect: a new thread_id points to an empty checkpoint, so there is no pending interrupt to resume. Use a new thread_id only to start an independent conversation.

Incorrect: previous_response_id with an approval response is the Responses API pattern for MCP approvals when you call Foundry directly. The LangGraph agent from create_prompt_agent resumes through Command.

stem:
Graphic Design Institute builds a long-running Agent Framework workflow in which an AgentExecutor wraps a FoundryAgent that uses server-side sessions. After restoring a checkpoint, the agent behaves as though its conversation state changed since the checkpoint was taken. The workflow must resume reliably from checkpoints.

What should you do?
choices: Implement a custom executor that manages the agent state
Share a single session between all AgentExecutor instances
Increase the frequency at which checkpoints are created
Switch the checkpoint storage to FileCheckpointStorage
explanation: When an AgentExecutor wraps an agent whose session state lives on the server, a workflow checkpoint cannot capture that state, so a restore can diverge from it. A custom executor that manages the agent state makes the state part of the checkpoint and resumes reliably.
rationale: Correct: a custom executor can keep the conversation state in workflow state that is checkpointed, so restoring a checkpoint restores the agent state as well, instead of relying on server-side sessions that changed.
Incorrect: sharing one session between AgentExecutor instances mixes the conversations of different agents and still keeps the state on the server, outside the checkpoint. Keep one session per agent.
Incorrect: more frequent checkpoints shrink the gap but cannot capture state that lives on the server, so a restore can still diverge. Tune frequency to limit lost work after a crash.
Incorrect: FileCheckpointStorage only changes where workflow checkpoints are stored. Server-side session state is still not part of them. Use file storage when checkpoints must survive restarts.

stem:
Wide World Importers uses the langchain-azure-ai package to compose a LangGraph solution with Foundry Agent Service. A developer adds the CodeInterpreterTool from langchain_azure_ai.agents.prebuilt.tools to a generic LangGraph tool node, and the graph fails when the model requests code execution. Data analysis must run in the Foundry sandbox.

What should you do?
choices: Pass the CodeInterpreterTool in the tools list of factory.create_prompt_agent
Wrap the CodeInterpreterTool in a local Python function and add it to the tool node
Retrieve the agent by using get_agent_node and add the CodeInterpreterTool to the tool node
Replace the CodeInterpreterTool with AzureAIDocumentIntelligenceTool
explanation: In langchain-azure-ai, tools in langchain_azure_ai.agents.prebuilt.tools are built-in Foundry tools that run server-side and work only with create_prompt_agent. Local tools run in a LangGraph tool node; built-in tools are passed to the prompt agent definition.
rationale: Correct: CodeInterpreterTool is a built-in tool that runs in the Foundry sandbox, and built-in tools work only when you pass them in the tools list of create_prompt_agent, so data analysis runs server-side.

Incorrect: wrapping the tool in a local function makes it a local tool that runs where your code runs, so analysis would not run in the Foundry sandbox. Wrap logic as a local tool for deterministic business code.

Incorrect: get_agent_node references an existing agent, and adding the tool to a separate tool node still treats it as a local tool, which fails. Use get_agent_node to reuse agents configured in Foundry.
Incorrect: AzureAIDocumentIntelligenceTool parses documents and acts like a local tool, so it neither executes analysis code nor runs in the sandbox. Use it to extract data from forms and invoices.

stem:
Northwind Traders migrates an AutoGen GraphFlow solution to Microsoft Agent Framework workflows. The new workflow must pause to wait for a credit officer decision, and it must continue from the same point after the host process restarts.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: Checkpointing lets the workflow continue from saved state after the host process restarts.
Agent Framework workflows deliver every message to every executor, in the same way as AutoGen GraphFlow broadcasts messages.
Request and response handling lets an executor pause the workflow until the credit officer decision is supplied.
explanation: Agent Framework workflows combine typed, edge-based message routing with built-in request and response handling and checkpointing. Request and response handling provides the human pause, and checkpointing provides durability across restarts, so long-running approvals need both.
rationale: Yes: checkpointing saves workflow state at superstep boundaries to a checkpoint storage. After a restart you restore a checkpoint by its ID and continue without repeating completed work.

No: Agent Framework workflows route messages along the edges that you define, so only connected executors receive a message. Broadcast-style delivery is an AutoGen GraphFlow behavior that the migration replaces.
Yes: an executor can request external input, which emits a request_info event and pauses the workflow until the application sends a response that references the request ID.

stem:
Lamna Healthcare Company has a validated patient-consent process that consists of three executors. The process must be reused inside several larger Agent Framework workflows. Each reuse must keep isolated input and output and its own independent state, and messages must not be broadcast between the outer and inner levels.

What should you do?
choices: Compose the consent process as a sub-workflow that runs as an executor in each larger workflow
Copy the three executors into each larger workflow and connect them with edges
Run the consent process as a group chat participant in each larger workflow
Expose the consent process as an A2A agent and call it from each larger workflow
explanation: Agent Framework supports sub-workflows: a complete workflow can run as an executor inside a larger workflow, with its own isolated input, output, and state. This lets you reuse a validated process without copying executors or exposing internal messages.
rationale: Correct: a sub-workflow runs as one executor in each larger workflow, so the consent process is reused unchanged, keeps isolated input, output, and state, and does not exchange internal messages with the outer level.

Incorrect: copying the executors duplicates the validated process, shares state with the outer workflow, and creates copies that must each be revalidated. Copy executors only when a variant must diverge.

Incorrect: a group chat participant takes turns in a shared conversation, so messages are visible to all participants and the consent process loses its isolated input and output. Use group chat for discussion.

Incorrect: an A2A agent adds a network hop and a separate deployment, and the consent process would run as a remote agent instead of a composed workflow. Use A2A to integrate agents owned by other teams.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. adds a sentiment pre-check in front of its support agents so that angry customers are routed to an escalation agent. The team wants to use a pre-trained Hugging Face model without additional training, and inference must use a GPU with batching when one is available.

Which Hugging Face Transformers component should you use?
choices: A Transformers pipeline for the sentiment analysis task
The Trainer class with TrainingArguments
The load_dataset function from the datasets library
DataCollatorWithPadding
explanation: Hugging Face Transformers pipelines wrap a pre-trained model and tokenizer for a task such as sentiment analysis. They need no training, use a GPU when one is available, and support batching, which makes them the simplest way to add a model-based check to an agent flow.
rationale: Correct: a sentiment-analysis pipeline loads a pre-trained model without training, runs on a GPU when available, and batches inputs, which matches the pre-check in front of the support agents.

Incorrect: the Trainer class with TrainingArguments fine-tunes a model on labeled data, which the team explicitly wants to avoid. Use it when a pre-trained model is not accurate enough for your domain.
Incorrect: load_dataset downloads and prepares datasets for training or evaluation. It does not run inference on customer messages. Use it to prepare data for fine-tuning.
Incorrect: DataCollatorWithPadding pads batches during training. It is a training utility and does not classify text. Use it with Trainer when inputs have different lengths.

stem:
Fabrikam, Inc. wants a small intent classifier that decides which specialist agent receives each request. The team has labeled examples and will fine-tune an open-source base model by using Hugging Face Transformers.

Which class should you use to load the base model for this task?
choices: AutoModelForSequenceClassification
AutoModelForTokenClassification
AutoModelForQuestionAnswering
AutoModelForCausalLM
explanation: Transformers provides task-specific Auto classes. Choose the class by output shape: one label per sequence uses AutoModelForSequenceClassification, one label per token uses AutoModelForTokenClassification, and text generation uses AutoModelForCausalLM.
rationale: Correct: intent classification assigns one label to each whole request, so AutoModelForSequenceClassification loads the base model with a sequence classification head sized for the intents.
Incorrect: AutoModelForTokenClassification assigns a label to every token, as in named entity recognition. Use it to extract entities such as order numbers from a request.
Incorrect: AutoModelForQuestionAnswering predicts an answer span inside a given context. Use it for extractive question answering over documents, not for routing requests.
Incorrect: AutoModelForCausalLM generates text token by token. It could classify through prompting, but it is larger and slower to fine-tune for this. Use it when the model must generate text.

stem:
Relecloud wants a retrieval agent to use an open-source Sentence-Transformers embedding model from the Hugging Face collection in the Foundry model catalog. The model is available in the current Foundry project.

Which deployment option should you use?
choices: Foundry Managed Compute
Global Batch
Global Provisioned
Data Zone Standard
explanation: Open-source Hugging Face models in the Foundry model catalog, such as Sentence-Transformers embedding models, are deployed to Foundry Managed Compute. Global Batch, Global Provisioned, and Data Zone Standard are deployment types for models sold directly by Azure, such as Azure OpenAI models.
rationale: Correct: Hugging Face models from the Foundry catalog are hosted on Foundry Managed Compute, which runs the open-source embedding model on dedicated compute in your project.
Incorrect: Global Batch is a deployment type for Azure OpenAI and other models sold directly by Azure, for asynchronous bulk jobs. It is not available for Hugging Face catalog models.
Incorrect: Global Provisioned reserves throughput units for models sold directly by Azure. Use it for predictable, high-volume Azure OpenAI traffic, not for Hugging Face models.
Incorrect: Data Zone Standard is a pay-per-token deployment type for models sold directly by Azure with data zone processing. Hugging Face catalog models do not use it.

stem:
Lucerne Publishing wants to deploy a permissively licensed Hugging Face chat model in the current Foundry experience for an editing agent. The model meets the Foundry support criteria and the project region supports it, but the model does not appear when the Available in my Project filter is enabled in the model catalog.

What should you do first?
choices: Request GPU quota for Foundry Managed Compute for a compatible accelerator type
Request a virtual machine core quota increase for the subscription
Assign the Foundry User role on the Foundry account to the developers
Change the deployment option filter of the model catalog to Global Batch
explanation: A Hugging Face model in Foundry appears under Available in my Project only when the project has quota for a compatible accelerator on Foundry Managed Compute. Request GPU quota for a compatible accelerator type first, and then deploy the model.
rationale: Correct: the filter shows only models that the project can deploy, and Foundry Managed Compute needs GPU quota for a compatible accelerator. Once that quota exists, the model appears and can be deployed.
Incorrect: a generic virtual machine core quota does not provide the accelerator quota that Foundry Managed Compute checks. Request VM core quota when you run self-managed virtual machines.

Incorrect: Foundry User grants access to use the project, but the filter hides the model because of missing compute quota, not missing permissions. Assign roles when users cannot open or use the project.
Incorrect: Global Batch is a deployment option for models sold directly by Azure, so changing the filter to it does not show Hugging Face models. Use it to find models that support batch jobs.

stem:
Wingtip Toys tries to deploy a Hugging Face model from the Azure Machine Learning model catalog for a product description agent. The deployment fails with an error that states that loading the model requires executing the configuration file in the model repository and setting trust_remote_code=True.

What should you do?
choices: Select an alternative model that uses Safetensors weights and does not require remote code
Set trust_remote_code to True in an environment variable of the deployment
Select a larger instance_type for the deployment
Add the missing Python libraries to a custom environment
explanation: Models that require trust_remote_code=True execute code from the model repository at load time, which Azure Machine Learning does not allow for catalog deployments. Choose an alternative model that does not require remote code, preferably with Safetensors weights.
rationale: Correct: the catalog does not deploy models that need remote code execution, so the fix is an alternative model that loads without trust_remote_code and ships Safetensors weights.

Incorrect: an environment variable does not override the deployment's block on remote code, and executing untrusted repository code is the risk the block prevents. Run such models only in your own vetted environment.
Incorrect: a larger instance type adds CPU, GPU, or memory, but the failure is about remote code execution, not resources. Choose a larger instance when the model runs out of memory.
Incorrect: adding libraries to a custom environment fixes missing dependencies, but the model would still require remote code. Use a custom environment when a model needs extra packages.

stem:
Trey Research fine-tunes a Hugging Face model on a single GPU to act as a domain classifier for its agents. Training with per_device_train_batch_size=16 fails with "OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory". The effective batch size must stay at 16. You change TrainingArguments to per_device_train_batch_size=4 and gradient_accumulation_steps=4.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: The change keeps the effective batch size at 16.
Setting fp16=True in TrainingArguments would increase the GPU memory that training needs.
The change lowers the GPU memory that each forward and backward pass needs.
explanation: On a memory-limited GPU, you reduce per_device_train_batch_size and raise gradient_accumulation_steps by the same factor to keep the effective batch size. Lower-precision training with fp16 and an 8-bit optimizer are further ways to reduce memory without changing the training objective.
rationale: Yes: the effective batch size is the per-device batch size multiplied by the gradient accumulation steps, so 4 x 4 keeps 16 samples per optimizer update on a single GPU.
No: fp16=True enables lower-precision training, which reduces memory use and is one of the documented fixes for CUDA out-of-memory errors. Keep full precision only when numeric stability requires it.
Yes: each pass now processes 4 samples instead of 16, so activations take less memory; gradients are summed over four passes before one optimizer step, which avoids the out-of-memory error.

stem:
Tailspin Toys uses a Hugging Face Transformers classifier on Azure Databricks to label millions of support transcripts. The labels feed an agent analytics dashboard daily. The input data is read several times for different experiments, and the scoring must scale across the cluster at low cost.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Run a preprocessing job that writes the cleaned transcripts to a Delta Lake table before the inference job
Apply the model by using an iterator pandas UDF that loads the model once and scores batches of rows
Apply the model by using a row-at-a-time Python UDF
Deploy the model from the HuggingFace registry to an Azure Machine Learning batch endpoint
Collect the transcripts to the driver node and score them with one Transformers pipeline
explanation: On Azure Databricks, store data that is read repeatedly in Delta Lake, and apply Transformers models at scale with an iterator pandas UDF that loads the model once per executor and scores batches. Avoid row-at-a-time UDFs and collecting data to the driver.
rationale: Correct: writing the cleaned transcripts to a Delta Lake table once lets every experiment read optimized data instead of repeating preprocessing, which is the recommended pattern for data that is read several times.
Correct: an iterator pandas UDF loads the model once per executor and scores batches of rows, so inference scales across the cluster with low overhead and low cost.

Incorrect: a row-at-a-time Python UDF pays serialization overhead for every row and can reload the model often, so it is slow and expensive for millions of transcripts. Use it only for light per-row logic.

Incorrect: models from the HuggingFace registry in Azure Machine Learning cannot be deployed to batch endpoints, and moving scoring off the Databricks cluster would add data movement anyway. Use an Azure Machine Learning batch endpoint for a model registered in the workspace.
Incorrect: collecting millions of transcripts to the driver puts all work on one node and can exhaust its memory, so it does not scale. Use the driver only for small samples during development.

stem:
Datum Corporation wants to summarize long documents overnight by using the facebook/bart-large-cnn Hugging Face model in Azure Machine Learning. A summarization agent reads the results the next morning. A batch endpoint named text-summarization-batch and a GPU compute cluster already exist, and deployment.yml references the model as azureml:bart-text-summarization@latest. An attempt to deploy the model directly from the HuggingFace registry to the batch endpoint failed.

Which five actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `az ml model create --name bart-text-summarization --path "model"`
`az ml job download --name $JOB_NAME --output-name score --download-path .`
Deploy the model to a managed online endpoint and have the summarization agent call it in a loop for each document.
`pipeline("summarization", model="facebook/bart-large-cnn").save_pretrained("model")`
`JOB_NAME=$(az ml batch-endpoint invoke --name text-summarization-batch --input data --input-type uri_folder --query name -o tsv)`
`az ml batch-endpoint create --file endpoint.yml --name text-summarization-batch`
`az ml batch-deployment create --file deployment.yml --endpoint-name text-summarization-batch --set-default`
explanation: Batch endpoints in Azure Machine Learning run asynchronous scoring jobs on a compute cluster that scales to zero, which suits overnight summarization. Hugging Face models are deployed to batch endpoints after you download them and register them in the workspace. The job flow is register, deploy, invoke, and then download the outputs.
rationale: Step 2: az ml model create registers the saved folder as bart-text-summarization, which is the name that deployment.yml references with @latest, so the deployment finds the model.
Step 5: az ml job download retrieves the score output of the finished job, to a local folder, so the summarization agent can read the summaries the next morning.

Incorrect: a managed online endpoint runs all day for real-time requests, so calling it in a loop for an overnight job costs more and needs custom retry logic. Use online endpoints when agents need low-latency answers.
Step 1: the model must first be downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub and saved to a local folder, because batch deployments need a model registered in the workspace, not a registry reference.
Step 4: az ml batch-endpoint invoke starts a batch scoring job over the input folder and returns the job name, which the download step needs to locate the outputs.

Incorrect: the endpoint text-summarization-batch already exists, and batch endpoint names must be unique in a region, so creating it again is unnecessary and fails. Create the endpoint only when none exists yet.
Step 3: az ml batch-deployment create deploys the registered model, scoring script, and environment to the existing endpoint; --set-default makes it the deployment that endpoint calls use.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank adds a Hugging Face model as a specialist in a multi-agent solution. Compliance requires that model weights are stored on Azure and are not downloaded from Hugging Face Hub at deployment time. The model is not gated, it is available in the current Foundry project, and the agent must call it through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Which deployment approach should you use?
choices: Deploy the model to Foundry Managed Compute in Foundry
Deploy the model to a managed online endpoint in Foundry (classic)
Deploy the model from the HuggingFace registry to an Azure Machine Learning managed online endpoint
Deploy the model to Azure Databricks Model Serving by loading it from Hugging Face Hub
explanation: Foundry Managed Compute deploys Hugging Face models from the Foundry catalog with weights that are stored on Azure instead of being downloaded from Hugging Face Hub at deployment time, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for agents.
rationale: Correct: Foundry Managed Compute serves the model from weights stored on Azure, so nothing is downloaded from Hugging Face Hub at deployment, and agents call it through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Incorrect: managed online endpoints in Foundry (classic) pull Hugging Face models from the Hub at deployment time, which breaks the compliance requirement. Use them only for existing classic deployments.

Incorrect: the HuggingFace registry in Azure Machine Learning downloads the model from Hugging Face Hub when it deploys, which breaks the requirement that weights are not downloaded at deployment time.

Incorrect: loading the model from Hugging Face Hub into Databricks Model Serving downloads the weights from the Hub, which the compliance rule forbids. Use Model Serving when the model already lives in Databricks.

stem:
Proseware, Inc. runs several Microsoft Agent Framework agents in Python and must add three reusable capabilities without modifying the agent or tool logic.

Which type of component should you use for each capability? To answer, drag the appropriate components to the correct capabilities. Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all.
choices: A context provider
Agent middleware
Chat middleware
Function middleware
targets: Capability1: log the name and duration of every tool call that the agents make
Capability2: audit the exact messages sent to the model, including the calls that send tool results back to the model
Capability3: stop a whole agent run before the model is called when the user message contains a blocked term, and return a fixed reply
explanation: Agent Framework has three middleware layers: agent middleware around the whole run, function middleware around each tool call, and chat middleware around each model call. Pick the layer whose scope matches the capability. Context providers inject context into runs and are not interception points.
rationale: Capability1 targets individual tool calls, and function middleware intercepts each function invocation with access to context.function.name, so it can time and log every call.
Capability2 needs every model request, and chat middleware runs inside the function invocation loop, so it sees each call to the model, including the ones that carry tool results.
Capability3 must decide before anything runs, and agent middleware wraps the whole run: it can set context.result and skip call_next() so the model is never called.
notes: Adds context, such as memories or instructions, to the agent before each run. Use it to enrich prompts with relevant context, not to intercept or block execution.
Wraps a complete agent run with access to messages, session, options, and result. Use it for run-level guards, auditing of complete runs, or result overrides.
Wraps each request to the AI model with access to raw messages and options. Use it when every model call, including tool-result round trips, must be inspected.
Wraps each tool invocation with access to the function, its arguments, and its result. Use it for tool logging, argument checks, or tool error fallbacks.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. must audit the exact messages that its Agent Framework agents send to the AI model. The audit must include every model call, including the calls that send tool results back to the model during a multi-turn tool calling sequence.

Which type of middleware should you implement?
choices: Chat middleware
Function middleware
Agent middleware registered at the run level
Agent middleware registered at the agent level
explanation: Chat middleware wraps each request to the AI model and runs inside the function invocation loop, so it sees every model call, including the follow-up calls that send tool results back. Agent middleware sees only the run as a whole.
rationale: Correct: chat middleware intercepts every request to the model with the exact messages, and because it runs inside the function calling loop, it also sees the calls that send tool results back.
Incorrect: function middleware intercepts tool invocations, not model requests, so it never sees the messages sent to the model. Use it to log or validate tool calls.
Incorrect: run-level agent middleware wraps one whole run and sees its input and final result, not each model call inside the tool loop. Use it for per-request run checks.
Incorrect: agent-level agent middleware wraps every run but still at run level, so the intermediate model calls with tool results are not visible. Use it for policies that apply to every run.

stem:
Wide World Importers has many Microsoft Agent Framework agents in Python that call an unstable shipping tool. When the tool raises a TimeoutError, every agent must return a consistent, user-friendly fallback message instead of an error. The behavior must be reusable across the solution, and the tool functions must not be modified.

Solution: You register function middleware on each agent that wraps await call_next() in a try block, catches TimeoutError, and sets context.result to the fallback message.

Does this meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: Middleware is the reusable place for cross-cutting exception handling in Agent Framework. Function middleware can catch a tool exception and override context.result, so the model receives a controlled message and the user gets a consistent fallback.
rationale: Correct: function middleware wraps every tool invocation, so catching TimeoutError around call_next() and setting context.result gives a consistent fallback for all agents without touching the tool code.

Incorrect: the solution does meet the goal. No would be right if the requirement were to retry the call or alert an operator, which needs extra logic in the middleware beyond setting a fallback result.

stem:
Adventure Works Cycles adds agent middleware in Python to an agent that uses Microsoft Agent Framework. After call_next(), the middleware must redact account numbers in the response by using a mask() function. The chat UI calls agent.run(..., stream=True), while a batch job calls agent.run() without streaming. One middleware function must handle both.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

```python
async def redact(context: AgentContext, call_next) -> None:
    await call_next()
    if context.result is None:
        return
    if [[1]]:
        original = context.result
        async def redacted_stream():
            async for update in original:
                yield [[2]]
        context.result = redacted_stream()
    else:
        context.result = AgentResponse(messages=[Message(role="assistant", contents=[mask(context.result.text)])])
```

targets.label: Box 1
why: Incorrect: context.result.messages exists only on a non-streaming AgentResponse. On a streaming result, which is an async generator, reading messages fails.
Correct: context.stream is True for streaming runs. In that case context.result is an async generator of updates, so the middleware must return a new generator instead of an AgentResponse.
Incorrect: context.metadata is a dictionary for passing data between middleware. It is truthy whenever any middleware stored data, so it cannot tell streaming from non-streaming runs.

targets.label: Box 2
why: Correct: a streaming override must yield AgentResponseUpdate chunks, the type that streaming callers consume. Wrapping the masked text in Content keeps the chunk format the chat UI expects.
Incorrect: AgentResponse is the complete non-streaming result type. Yielding it from a stream gives the UI objects of the wrong type, which is the failure the redaction must avoid.
Incorrect: yielding a plain string breaks consumers that read update.text or update.contents. A string is fine only as content inside an AgentResponseUpdate.

explanation: The type of context.result depends on the run mode: an AgentResponse for non-streaming runs and an async generator of AgentResponseUpdate chunks for streaming runs. Middleware that overrides results checks context.stream and replaces the result with the matching type, so one function serves both callers.

stem:
Wide World Importers has many Microsoft Agent Framework agents in Python that call an unstable shipping tool. When the tool raises a TimeoutError, every agent must return a consistent, user-friendly fallback message instead of an error. The behavior must be reusable across the solution, and the tool functions must not be modified.

Solution: You add a try/except block inside the shipping tool function that returns the fallback message when a TimeoutError occurs.

Does this meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: Error handling inside each tool duplicates logic and couples tools to user-facing messages. Middleware centralizes the behavior and leaves tool code unchanged, which is why it is the reusable pattern for exception handling.
rationale: Incorrect: a try/except block in the tool would return a fallback, but it modifies the tool function, which the goal forbids, and it does not give a reusable pattern for other tools.
Correct: the solution does not meet the goal. Handling errors inside a tool is reasonable when only that one tool needs a special fallback and you own its code; here middleware is required.

stem:
VanArsdel, Ltd. hosts a multi-tenant Agent Framework solution. Tools must receive the tenant ID of the authenticated caller for authorization checks. The model must not be able to supply or change the tenant ID, and the solution must work for every agent.

What should you do?
choices: Set the tenant ID in context.function_invocation_kwargs in agent middleware
Add a tenant_id parameter to each tool so that the model supplies the value
Add the tenant ID of the caller to the instructions of each agent
Append a message that contains the tenant ID in chat middleware
explanation: Values that the model must not control, such as a tenant ID for authorization, belong in runtime context rather than in tool parameters or prompts. Agent middleware can set context.function_invocation_kwargs, which are forwarded to tools and hidden from the model.
rationale: Correct: function_invocation_kwargs are forwarded to tools at run time and are not part of the tool schema, so the model cannot supply or change the tenant ID, and one agent middleware applies to every agent.

Incorrect: a tenant_id tool parameter appears in the schema, so the model supplies the value and could change it, for example through prompt injection. Use parameters only for values the model should decide.
Incorrect: a tenant ID in the instructions is text the model reads; the model still has to pass it to tools and could alter it. Use instructions to guide behavior, never to carry authorization data.
Incorrect: a message appended in chat middleware is again model-visible text, so the model can ignore or change the value it passes to tools. Use chat middleware to inspect or adjust model requests.

stem:
Wide World Importers has many Microsoft Agent Framework agents in Python that call an unstable shipping tool. When the tool raises a TimeoutError, every agent must return a consistent, user-friendly fallback message instead of an error. The behavior must be reusable across the solution, and the tool functions must not be modified.

Solution: You set include_detailed_errors to True in the function invocation configuration of each chat client.

Does this meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: By default, a failed tool returns a generic error result to the model, and include_detailed_errors adds the exception text. Neither controls what the user sees; a consistent fallback needs middleware that overrides the result.
rationale: Incorrect: include_detailed_errors only adds the exception type and message to the tool result that the model sees. The model still phrases its own reply, so the fallback is not consistent, and exception text can leak sensitive data.

Correct: the solution does not meet the goal. Enable include_detailed_errors only on trusted channels when the model or a developer needs the error details for diagnosis, not to produce a fixed user message.

stem:
Northwind Traders needs audit logging for every run of its Agent Framework agents. For one troubleshooting session, the support team also wants verbose diagnostic logging that applies to a single request only. The solution must keep the agent logic unchanged.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Register the audit logging middleware at the agent level when you create the agent
Pass the diagnostic logging middleware in the middleware parameter of agent.run() for the request
Add audit logging code to each tool function
Register the diagnostic logging middleware at the agent level and remove it after the session
Register the diagnostic logging middleware as chat middleware on the chat client
explanation: Agent-level middleware is registered when the agent is created and applies to every run; run-level middleware is passed to agent.run() and applies to that request only. Agent-level middleware wraps run-level middleware, so both can be combined without changing agent logic.
rationale: Correct: middleware registered at the agent level runs for every run of the agent, so audit logging is applied consistently without changing the agent logic.
Correct: middleware passed in the middleware parameter of agent.run() applies only to that request, which gives verbose diagnostics for the troubleshooting session without affecting other runs.
Incorrect: logging code inside each tool function changes tool logic and only captures tool calls, not complete runs. Add logging inside a tool only for details that only the tool knows.

Incorrect: registering diagnostics at the agent level applies them to every request until someone removes them, which is not limited to one request. Use agent-level registration for permanent behavior.
Incorrect: chat middleware on the chat client applies to every model call that uses the client, so it is not scoped to one request. Use chat middleware to inspect model requests across runs.
